extra.message: No USER directive is specified in the Dockerfile, so the application runs as the root user inside the container.

The application is configured to bind to 0.0.0.0, making it accessible from all network interfaces. This is combined with the --host argument defaulting to 127.0.0.1 in the code but overridden to 0.0.0.0 in Docker.

A file named 'secret.txt' exists in the docs directory, accessible via the path traversal vulnerability. The content reads 'This is super secret...' indicating it may contain confidential information.
A file named 'secret.txt' containing 'This is super secret...' exists in the docs directory which is accessible via the application's path traversal vulnerability and potentially via direct access.
SSL/TLS encryption is disabled by default (--ssl defaults to false). All traffic is transmitted in cleartext unless explicitly enabled.
The SSL configuration explicitly allows SSLv3 (a severely deprecated protocol vulnerable to the POODLE attack) and disables compression and cipher server preference controls.
The SSL context explicitly removes the OP_NO_SSLv3 flag, re-enabling the insecure SSLv3 protocol which is vulnerable to the POODLE attack.

The SSL context configuration unsets `OP_NO_SSLv3` (enabling the broken SSLv3 protocol vulnerable to POODLE attack), unsets `OP_NO_COMPRESSION` (enabling TLS compression vulnerable to CRIME attack), and unsets `OP_CIPHER_SERVER_PREFERENCE` (allowing clients to negotiate weak ciphers).
When an exception occurs in the main loop, the exception message is printed to stdout, potentially exposing sensitive error details to console viewers.
No monetary or stock-related operations exist in this codebase that could be exploited via unvalidated amounts or quantities.
User-supplied 'id' parameter is directly concatenated into SQL query without parameterization. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL by manipulating the 'id' query parameter.
SQL OperationalError exceptions are caught and returned directly to the user, exposing database schema information and query internals.
The SQL injection result includes the 'session' column values (session tokens) rendered in an HTML table. This exposes active session tokens in the response.
Database column values returned by the SQL query are rendered directly into HTML table cells without HTML escaping via .format(). User-controlled data from the database is output unsanitized.
The 'msg' parameter from user input is returned directly in the HTTP response without any HTML escaping or sanitization.

The 'msg' parameter from user input is returned directly in the HTTP response without any HTML escaping or sanitization. The content is later rendered in the template via {content} which outputs raw HTML.
The comment submission endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to flood the guestbook with unlimited comments.
User-supplied 'comment' parameter is stored directly in the database without any sanitization or escaping.

The SELECT query that retrieves comments for display does not use parameterized queries, though in this case no user input is directly concatenated. However, the SELECT is vulnerable if the id parameter were to affect it.
User comments are stored in the database and then rendered in an HTML table without HTML escaping. The column values are directly injected into the HTML via .format().

The UnvalidatedRedirect.run() takes a user-supplied 'path' parameter and uses it in a JavaScript redirect without any validation. An attacker can redirect users to arbitrary external URLs, which is useful for phishing attacks.

The UnvalidatedRedirect.run() method takes a user-controlled 'path' parameter and injects it directly into a JavaScript string context without any escaping. An attacker can break out of the string context by injecting a single quote and craft arbitrary JavaScript. This is both an open redirect and XSS vulnerability.
The 'path' parameter is used directly in a JavaScript redirect without any validation. An attacker can redirect users to arbitrary external URLs.

The UnvalidatedRedirect.run() injects a user-supplied 'path' parameter directly into a JavaScript string literal inside a <script> tag via str.format(). The path is inserted into a JavaScript window.location.replace() call without any escaping.

The user-controlled 'domain' parameter is passed to subprocess.check_output() with shell=True. Even though the command prefix is 'host' or 'nslookup', an attacker can inject shell metacharacters (;, |, `, $()) through the domain parameter to execute arbitrary commands.

The subprocess.check_output call has no timeout parameter. An attacker can provide a domain or command that hangs indefinitely (e.g., a 'sleep' command), exhausting server resources and causing a denial of service.

The CommandInjection.run() method executes the 'host' or 'nslookup' command with the user-supplied 'domain' parameter using subprocess.check_output() with shell=True. The domain parameter is not sanitized, allowing arbitrary command injection.
User-controlled base64-decoded data is passed directly to pickle.loads(). Pickle deserialization can execute arbitrary code during the loading process via the __reduce__ method of crafted objects.
User-controlled 'path' parameter is passed directly to os.path.abspath() and then open() without validation. An attacker can read arbitrary files on the server.

The user-controlled 'path' parameter is passed to open() after os.path.abspath(). However, os.path.abspath() does NOT prevent directory traversal - it only resolves '..' segments. An attacker can use '../../etc/passwd' to read arbitrary files on the system.

The urllib.request.urlopen call has no timeout specified. An attacker can provide a URL to a slow endpoint or a server that hangs, causing the request thread to block indefinitely and exhausting server resources.

If the user-supplied 'path' parameter contains '://', it is passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen() without validation. An attacker can make the server fetch arbitrary URLs, including internal resources.

The SessionFixation.run() allows a user to set the SESSIONID cookie to an arbitrary value via the 'session' query parameter. An attacker can set a known session ID and then trick a victim into using that same session ID, allowing session hijacking after the victim authenticates.
An attacker can set a user's session ID to a value chosen by the attacker via the 'session' GET parameter. The session ID stored in the cookie is overwritten without any validation.

The SessionFixation.run() method takes a user-controlled 'path' parameter and injects it directly into a JavaScript string context without any escaping. An attacker can break out of the string context and execute arbitrary JavaScript.
User-supplied 'path' parameter is used directly in a JavaScript redirect without any validation, allowing open redirect to arbitrary URLs.
The 'path' parameter in SessionFixation.run() is used in a client-side redirect without validation, allowing open redirect via the path parameter.

User personally identifiable information (first name, last name, email) is returned in the response body when a valid session cookie is provided. This data is displayed in the HTML response visible to anyone with the session ID.

The SessionHijacking.run() renders user data (username, firstname, lastname, email) from the database into HTML via str.format() without escaping. This user data originates from database and could contain malicious content.
The authentication/login endpoint (AuthBypass.run()) has no rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or exponential backoff, allowing unlimited brute-force password attempts.

The AuthBypass.run() reads username and password from URL query parameters (GET request). This causes passwords to be exposed in server logs, browser history, referrer headers, and visible in the URL.
The hardcoded credentials are compared as plaintext strings. Additionally, the SQL query at line 289 compares passwords as plaintext in WHERE clause: password='" + password + "'
The AuthBypass.run() contains hardcoded credentials 'dsvpwa'/'dsvpwa' that skip the database query and authenticate as an admin user. These credentials are publicly visible in source code.

User passwords are stored in plaintext in the SQLite database and compared directly against user input in SQL queries. No password hashing (bcrypt, argon2, etc.) is used, meaning a database compromise reveals all passwords.

The 'password' parameter is directly concatenated into the SQL query string. While 'username' is sanitized with regex, 'password' is not sanitized at all, allowing SQL injection through the password field.

When a SQL injection attempt causes an OperationalError, the exception message is returned to the user unescaped. This reveals database schema information and confirms the SQL injection vulnerability is exploitable.

After successful authentication (line 294), the user's existing session ID from the cookie is stored in the database at line 297 (`cursor.execute("UPDATE users SET session = ? WHERE id = ?", (session, user[0]))`). The session ID is never regenerated after login. An attacker can force a known session ID on the victim (e.g., via the session fixation attack on the same page or via links), and after the victim logs in, the attacker can hijack the session using the known session ID.

After successful authentication, the session ID is stored in the database (UPDATE users SET session=?) but the cookie's SESSIONID is NOT regenerated. Combined with the SessionFixation attack class that allows setting SESSIONID via a parameter, an attacker can fixate a session and hijack it after the victim logs in.
The email/settings update endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly change a user's email address.

The email update functionality in XSRequestForgery.run() uses HTTP GET requests with no CSRF token. The session is authenticated via cookie, but there is no CSRF protection. An attacker can craft a link or image tag that triggers a state change when a logged-in victim visits it.

The XSRequestForgery.run() renders user firstname, lastname, and email from the database into HTML form input values via str.format() without escaping. If these values contain malicious content (e.g., injected via the email update at line 324), this leads to stored XSS.
The account deletion endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing rapid deletion of accounts.
The account deletion functionality in Clickjacking.run() uses HTTP GET requests with no CSRF token. An attacker can trick a logged-in user into clicking a link that deletes their account.
SSLv3 is explicitly enabled by removing the OP_NO_SSLv3 flag from the SSL context options. SSLv3 is vulnerable to the POODLE attack (CVE-2014-3566).

The SSL context explicitly enables SSLv3 by clearing the OP_NO_SSLv3 flag. SSLv3 is deprecated and vulnerable to the POODLE attack (CVE-2014-3566), which allows plaintext recovery from encrypted connections.
The template parameter is used to construct a file path by concatenating 'templates/' with a user-influenced route value. No validation prevents directory traversal.
The URL path from the HTTP request is used directly in open() with only './' prepended. An attacker can use path traversal sequences like '/../../etc/passwd' to read arbitrary files on the server.

The HTTP request line (self.requestline) is logged directly via sys.stdout.write without sanitization. An attacker can inject fake log entries, newlines, or escape sequences by including them in the HTTP request path or headers.
The log_error function uses printf-style formatting (%s) with user-controlled data (args), enabling log injection.
The log_error method passes user-controlled data (format%args) to sys.stderr.write. The format string vulnerability occurs when user input is included in the logging output without sanitization.
The log_message function uses printf-style formatting (%args) where args come from the HTTP request. This can inject arbitrary content into logs, allowing log forging.
The do_BDR method handles a custom HTTP method and executes the request path as a shell command when risk >= 3. This is effectively an active debug backdoor that gives attackers RCE.
The BDR command execution endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to repeatedly execute arbitrary commands without restriction.
The subprocess.check_output call in do_BDR has no timeout. An attacker can send an HTTP request that executes a long-running command (e.g., 'sleep 1000'), hanging the server thread.
The raw URL path (stripping leading '/') is passed directly to subprocess.check_output() with shell=True. Any BDR HTTP request to a path like '/;id' would execute the 'id' command on the server.

When a session is created for a new visitor at /login, the session cookie is loaded into the SimpleCookie object but no security attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) are set before the cookie is sent to the client.
Session tokens are generated using random.sample() which uses the Mersenne Twister PRNG (not cryptographically secure). The token is 20 characters of alphanumeric, making it predictable.

Session tokens are generated using random.sample() from the random module, which uses a Mersenne Twister PRNG that is not cryptographically secure. An attacker who observes multiple session tokens can predict future tokens.

When an exception occurs during handler content generation, the raw exception message (str(ex)) is returned to the user in the HTTP response body. This can leak internal implementation details, stack information, or database error messages.

When sending session cookies to the client, only the 'path' attribute is set. No 'HttpOnly' flag is applied, making session cookies accessible to client-side JavaScript. This enables session theft via XSS attacks.

The application does not send an X-Frame-Options header, making it possible to render the application in an iframe on other sites. Combined with the clickjacking attack class (Clickjacking.run()), this enables clickjacking attacks.
Session cookies are sent without the SameSite attribute, making the application vulnerable to CSRF attacks that are not mitigated by browser SameSite protections.
Session cookies are sent without the 'Secure' flag, meaning they will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. This allows session hijacking via network sniffing on non-HTTPS connections.
No X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors CSP directive is set, allowing the application to be embedded in iframes on attacker-controlled pages.
The Content-Security-Policy header is set to `default-src * 'unsafe-inline'` which allows loading resources from any origin and allows inline scripts, completely defeating the purpose of CSP.

User passwords are loaded from XML (users.xml) and stored in the SQLite database as plaintext. The database schema has a 'password TEXT' column with no hashing. All user passwords are stored in cleartext.
User passwords are loaded from an XML file (./db/users.xml) in plaintext and stored directly in the database without hashing.
The password column in the users table is defined as plain TEXT with no hashing or encryption. Passwords are stored in cleartext in the database.
The JavaScript code parses a 'lang' parameter from the URL hash fragment and writes unsanitized content directly into the page using document.write().

The login form uses the GET method instead of POST, causing the username and password to be transmitted as query parameters in the URL. This exposes credentials in server logs, browser history, referrer headers, and network logs.
